dataset_family: WHICAP (Washington Heights-Inwood Columbia Aging Project), Northern Manhattan, random Medicare sampling in 1992/1999/2009 waves; 2,903 cognitively normal at baseline, 752 incident MCI, 480 with a follow-up visit after incident MCI
method_family: Community-cohort epidemiology: Cox regression of incident MCI (with dementia-before-MCI also counted as an event) and modified Poisson regression of diagnostic status at the first visit after incident MCI, with dichotomous CES-D-10 depressive symptoms (cut-off 4) as one of many predictors; multiple imputation for missing data
what_it_shows: Dichotomous depressive symptoms did not significantly predict incident MCI (age/wave-adjusted HR 1.19, 0.99-1.43, p 0.069; full model HR 1.01, p 0.910). Among people with incident MCI, depressive symptoms predicted progression to dementia rather than classification as cognitively normal at the next visit (RR 1.84 separate model, 1.80 full model). Depression severity is never analysed as a continuous or graded score, and there are no brain measures.
why: Angevaare et al., Neurology 2022;98:e15-e26. The PDF title and authors match the summaries.md block and the map entry. The paper supports no clause of the Table A1 row. First clause (depression status is associated with MCI): not demonstrated; the age/wave-adjusted hazard ratio has a confidence interval crossing 1 (p 0.069) and the fully adjusted one is null (p 0.910). The text nonetheless lists 'having more depressive symptoms' among the separate-model predictors of higher incident-MCI risk, which the table's p 0.069 does not support; this is a text-table inconsistency in the source. The incident-MCI event count (1,053) also includes 301 who reached dementia without an intermediate MCI diagnosis. Severity clause: not testable, because depression was coded only as present or absent (CES-D-10 >= 4). Conversion: the only depression-prognosis result is POSITIVE for status (RR 1.80, 1.06-3.06, full model), which points against the null side rather than for it, although as a status measure it is not severity grading either; the comparator is those classified cognitively normal at follow-up (sustained MCI is a separate contrast, where depressive symptoms were null, RR 1.04). Limits: CES-D missing for 24% at baseline and 30% in the MCI-course sample (imputed); only 480 of 752 incident MCI had a follow-up; follow-up after incident MCI averaged 2.4 years; 62 progressed to dementia. Independence: WHICAP, no overlap in sample, site or authors with P-643, P-647, P-788, P-974 or any round-1 candidate. Not a preprint. Symbols in quotes are transliterated to ASCII.

quotes.quote: Depressive symptoms were assessed at each visit with the 10-item version of the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale.27 For the analyses, a dichotomous variable indicating significant depressive symptoms using the conventional cutoff score of 4 was created.

Due to interval censoring, the onset of MCI was set at the midpoint between the last visit with normal cognition and the first visit with MCI or the first visit with a dementia diagnosis in those cases in which dementia diagnosis was not preceded by MCI.

In a series of models that examined the individual relationships between each predictor and incident MCI, we observed higher risk of incident MCI with being of Hispanic ethnicity, being an APOE e4 carrier, having higher medical burden, and having more depressive symptoms [...] However, when all predictors were entered into the full model together, ethnic background, occupation, and depressive symptoms dropped out of the model
(Table 3, Separate models | Full model | Sensitivity analysis; n = 2,902, 1,053 events) Depressive symptoms 1.19 (0.99-1.43), p = 0.069 | 1.01 (0.83-1.24), p = 0.910 | 1.05 (0.89-1.24), p = 0.570

Higher risk of progression to dementia relative to classification as cognitively normal at follow-up was associated with having multidomain MCI, antidepressant use, and depressive symptoms in both separate models and the full model.

(Table 5; Sustained MCI vs cognitively normal separate | full ; Functional decline vs cognitively normal separate | full ; Dementia vs cognitively normal, N = 292 [62, 230], separate | full) Depressive symptoms 1.02 (0.63-1.65), p = 0.929 | 1.04 (0.64-1.69) p = 0.883 ; 2.10 (1.09-4.04), p = 0.027 | 1.67 (0.81-3.42), p = 0.160 ; 1.84 (1.03-3.28), p = 0.038 | 1.80 (1.06-3.06), p = 0.030
(Table 1 note) 24% missing data on depressive symptoms.
(Table 4 note) 30% missing data on depressive symptoms.

The presence of depressive symptoms and antidepressant use were associated with higher incident MCI risk in the model adjusted only for age and recruitment cohort, but this association did not survive in the fully adjusted model.

Although this extensive cohort allowed study of follow-up after incident MCI, the proportion with follow-up after incident MCI is relatively small, and the follow-up time after incident MCI is relatively short.
